skills.name: Describe the chemical properties of hydrogen sulphide

note.text:
Hydrogen sulphide is a weak acid, a reducing agent and it burns in air.
• Weak acid: its solution turns blue litmus red. With alkalis it gives sulphides: H2S + 2NaOH → Na2S + 2H2O.
• Burning: in plenty of air, 2H2S + 3O2 → 2SO2 + 2H2O (blue flame). In a limited supply, 2H2S + O2 → 2S + 2H2O, leaving a yellow deposit.
• Reducing agent: it is oxidised to sulphur by many oxidising agents. With acidified potassium manganate(VII) the purple colour goes and sulphur appears; with chlorine water the colour goes; with sulphur dioxide: SO2 + 2H2S → 3S + 2H2O.
• With metal salts it gives coloured sulphide precipitates, used in analysis: lead(II) nitrate gives black PbS. Lead(II) ethanoate paper turning black is the test for the gas.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to describe hydrogen sulphide as a weak acid, a reducing agent and a gas that burns, and give the test for it.
Builds on: Lesson {5} (preparing {formula('H2S')}) and Lesson {4} (redox reactions of {formula('SO2')}).
Leads to: Lesson {7} (the sulphides themselves) and the use of {formula('H2S')} in analysis.

sections.heading: Burning and acidity
sections.text:
Hydrogen sulphide burns in air with a blue flame, and what it gives depends on how much oxygen it has.
• Plenty of air: {2}{formula('H2S')} + {3}{formula('O2')} → {2}{formula('SO2')} + {2}{formula('H2O')}.
• Limited air: {2}{formula('H2S')} + {formula('O2')} → {2}S + {2}{formula('H2O')}, leaving a yellow deposit.
In water it is a weak acid: the solution turns blue litmus red, and with sodium hydroxide it gives a sulphide:
{formula('H2S')} + {2}{formula('NaOH')} → {formula('Na2S')} + {2}{formula('H2O')}.

sections.heading: A reducing agent, and the test
sections.text:
Hydrogen sulphide gives up hydrogen easily, so it is a good reducing agent. It is itself oxidised to sulphur, which appears as a pale yellow deposit:
• acidified potassium manganate(VII): purple → colourless, with sulphur;
• chlorine water: the colour goes, with sulphur;
• sulphur dioxide: {formula('SO2')} + {2}{formula('H2S')} → {3}S + {2}{formula('H2O')}. Here {formula('SO2')} is the oxidising agent.
With solutions of metal salts it gives sulphides of different colours, which is why it is used in analysis:
{formula('Pb(NO3)2')} + {formula('H2S')} → {formula('PbS')} + {2}{formula('HNO3')}, a BLACK precipitate.
The test for the gas is damp lead(II) ethanoate paper, which turns black.

key_words.meaning: an acid only slightly split into ions in water
a substance that gives electrons or hydrogen to another
an insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed
test paper that turns black with hydrogen sulphide

mistake.wrong: hydrogen sulphide burning in limited air gives sulphur dioxide
mistake.why: With too little oxygen, only the hydrogen is oxidised, leaving the sulphur behind.

worked_example.problem: Explain, with equations, what happens when hydrogen sulphide burns in plenty of air and in a limited supply of air.
steps: In plenty of air there is enough oxygen to oxidise both the hydrogen and the sulphur.
In a limited supply there is only enough oxygen for the hydrogen.
{2}{formula('H2S')} + {formula('O2')} → {2}S + {2}{formula('H2O')}, leaving a yellow deposit of sulphur.
worked_example.answer: plenty of air gives {formula('SO2')} and water; limited air gives sulphur and water

pick.q: Hydrogen sulphide burns in plenty of air. What is formed?
pick.r: Sulphur dioxide and water
e: Sulphur and water are formed when the air supply is LIMITED.
Burning joins the gas with oxygen; it does not split it into its elements.
{formula('SO3')} is not formed by simple burning, and the hydrogen is oxidised to water.
pick.y: {2}{formula('H2S')} + {3}{formula('O2')} → {2}{formula('SO2')} + {2}{formula('H2O')}, with a blue flame.

pick.q: Hydrogen sulphide burns in a limited supply of air. What is seen?
pick.r: A yellow deposit of sulphur forms
w: The flame goes out at once
A brown gas is given off
e: No white solid is formed in this reaction.
It still burns; the limited air changes the product, not whether it burns.
A brown gas is nitrogen dioxide, which is not formed here.
pick.y: {2}{formula('H2S')} + {formula('O2')} → {2}S + {2}{formula('H2O')}: with too little oxygen the sulphur is not oxidised.

pick.q: Why is hydrogen sulphide described as a reducing agent?
pick.r: It gives up its hydrogen or its electrons, and is itself oxidised to sulphur
w: It adds oxygen to other substances
It is an acid in water
e: Adding oxygen is what an OXIDISING agent does.
Being an acid is a separate property; it has nothing to do with reduction.
Density has nothing to do with being a reducing agent.
pick.y: With most oxidising agents, {formula('H2S')} is oxidised and a pale yellow deposit of sulphur appears.

pick.q: Hydrogen sulphide is passed into lead(II) nitrate solution. What is seen?
pick.r: A black precipitate of lead(II) sulphide
e: Lead(II) sulphide is black, not white.
A precipitate forms rather than a coloured solution.
The change is clear and is used as a test for the gas.
pick.y: {formula('Pb(NO3)2')} + {formula('H2S')} → {formula('PbS')} + {2}{formula('HNO3')}: lead sulphide is black.

pick.q: Which test paper shows that a gas is hydrogen sulphide?
pick.r: Filter paper moistened with lead(II) ethanoate, which turns black
w: Damp red litmus paper, which turns blue
Starch iodide paper, which turns blue
Filter paper moistened with limewater, which turns milky
e: {formula('H2S')} is acidic, so it turns BLUE litmus red, and that is not a specific test.
Starch iodide paper is used for chlorine and other oxidising gases.
Limewater is the test for carbon dioxide.
pick.y: Lead(II) ethanoate paper turning black shows the black lead sulphide.

pick.q: Hydrogen sulphide is bubbled into a solution of sulphur dioxide. What is seen, and which gas is oxidised?
pick.r: A yellow deposit of sulphur; the hydrogen sulphide is oxidised
w: A yellow deposit; the sulphur dioxide is oxidised
A white precipitate; neither is oxidised
No change; the two gases do not react
e: {formula('SO2')} is the oxidising agent here, so it is REDUCED, not oxidised.
A yellow solid, not a white one, is formed, and a redox reaction does take place.
The two react readily and the sulphur formed is easy to see.
pick.y: {formula('SO2')} + {2}{formula('H2S')} → {3}S + {2}{formula('H2O')}: {formula('H2S')} loses hydrogen, so it is oxidised.
